Text:
A widow in New England kept on in prayer, day and night. She had two daughters who earned their living with their needles. One winter day they were so taken up finishing work that had been on their hands a long time that they had not laid in ordinary supplies.

They found themselves in a snowstorm, food and fuel almost gone, far from neighbors, and with no way to get what they needed.

The account says the supply came, and the widow turned to her unbelieving daughters and asked them what they thought now.

They were speechless. From that hour, the book says, they learned to trust the One who supplies those who trust Him.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE STORM HAD THEM SHUT IN. THE WOOD AND THE FLOUR WERE ALMOST GONE.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Widow's Wood and Flour.--The Unbelieving Ones Made Speechless."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
In the latter part of November 1864 a woman was traveling from New Hampshire toward Indiana with her aged father and two small girls. A freight smash-up put them behind. Conductor after conductor told her they could not make the down train at Toledo. One said that conductor was never known to wait a second past the time, and that the depot fire would be out until Sunday evening.

She covered her eyes and prayed, "O, God, if thou art my Father, and I am thy child, put it into the heart of that conductor to wait till we get there." She fell asleep, not realizing it would be answered.

At Toledo the other conductor was still there. He said he had waited a whole half hour, a thing he had never done. Both conductors helped her father across. She handed over the baggage checks and had none back before the car started. The conductor later handed her the checks and said the baggage would not be there until Monday morning. They had waited so long there was no time to load it.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: EVERY CONDUCTOR SAID THE TRAIN WOULD NOT WAIT. IT WAITED HALF AN HOUR.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Another Instance of Superhuman Control of the Locomotive, in Answer to Prayer."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 2, "Thanks Be Unto God," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"O LORD God, help us now really to worship Thee. We would thank Thee for this occasion. We bless Thy name for setting apart this hallowed season. Lord, wilt Thou shut the door upon the world for us? Help us to forget our cares. Enable us to rise clean out of this world. May we get rid of all its down-dragging tendencies. May the attractions of these grossest things be gone and do Thou catch us away to Thyself."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: O LORD GOD, HELP US NOW REALLY TO WORSHIP THEE
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A clergyman on the Fleming Circuit in Kentucky was staying with a family named Bowers. The next day he was to ride five miles and preach at eleven at a church called Mount Olivet.

All Saturday afternoon and night he could not fix on a passage. One passage, two or three clauses of which he already had in memory, stood in his mind as if written in capital letters. He turned to it as soon as he could find it.

The next morning Sister Bowers told him she had agreed with herself that if he went to their own church she would stay, but if he went to Mount Olivet she would go, and she had prayed the Lord would take that text. She said she kept praying until she heard him read it out at Mount Olivet.

He then told Brother and Sister Bowers what the text had cost him the day before.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: ALL SATURDAY HE COULD NOT SETTLE ON A TEXT. ONE LINE WOULD NOT LEAVE HIM.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Remarkable Prayer Concerning a Remarkable Text."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 40:

"And it is in compassion to us that thou holdest back the face of that throne, and spreadest a cloud upon it."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: What is he sparing us by not showing us everything?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 40. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
In 1839 a sailor on the brig Pandora, Captain G., bound from Savannah to Boston with cotton, told this at a Sunday meeting in Repository Hall on January 25, 1874. The Christian printed it afterward.

Off the Virginia coast, about twenty-five miles from Chesapeake Bay, a gale met them. Saturday evening, December 21, the wind was gentle from the south. At midnight it veered east and kept rising. By four on Sunday morning the brig was under close-reefed topsails and foresail. Then every stitch of canvas came in.

He said that after they prayed, the wind that had been driving them toward danger turned and wafted them out into deep water. The Pandora swung to the helm and they laid her course again for port. Some who had mocked at prayers admitted that God had delivered them.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: OFF VIRGINIA THE GALE TOOK EVERY STITCH OF CANVAS. THEN THE WIND TURNED AND HELD.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Storm Made Calm."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A young preacher in Massachusetts, in a field that paid little, had laid aside fifteen dollars for a coat he needed. Before he could buy it, a charitable object was put before him. He had thought of giving ten dollars. He gave it, and trusted the Lord for the coat.

Within two or three days he was at his mother's house in another town. She noticed the coat and said he seemed to need a new one. He said he would get one as soon as he had the means.

She told him there was a coat upstairs that his brother had had made not over two weeks before, worn only once, because it was made too small. His brother had said he might have it. It fitted exactly. The brother was larger than he was, and not particularly interested in the Lord's work. The book says nothing short of Providence could have made a coat measured for one of them fit the other.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE GAVE AWAY THE MONEY FOR HIS COAT. HIS MOTHER SAID THERE WAS ONE UPSTAIRS.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The New Coat That Fitted Exactly."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 3, "The Love Without Measure or End," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"LORD, we would come to Thee, but do Thou come to us. Draw us and we will run after Thee. Blessed Spirit, help our infirmities, for we know not what we should pray for as we ought. Come, Holy Spirit, and give right thoughts and right utterance that we may all be able to pray in the common prayer, the whole company feeling that for each one there is a portion."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: LORD, WE WOULD COME TO THEE, BUT DO THOU COME TO US
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
About 1853, near the middle of a Canadian winter, a minister wrote The Christian about a run of snow, high wind, and severe cold. His winter wood was two miles off, on a road running north and south, open to the west wind.

He had very little to do with, and he could not bear much fatigue or the severe cold. He had found a man to chop and help him load, and he had engaged a horse from one neighbor.

He asked the Lord for a break in that wind. What came, he said, other people called a nice spell of weather or a lucky thing. To him it was the loving-kindness of the Lord. Years later he wrote it down so others in trouble would call on the Lord, and as thanks to the One who never said to the house of Jacob, seek ye my face in vain.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE HAD TO HAUL A WINTER OF WOOD TWO MILES INTO THE WEST WIND.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Hushed Tempest."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 48:

"What is man that thou art thus mindful of him, and the son of man that thou visitest him? and dost thus magnify him."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Why would he be mindful of us?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 48. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: Johnny Hall's mother had nothing to give him for supper. He prayed that line with her, and a gentleman came asking her to keep his two motherless boys.
Alt text(s): Image reading: Give us this day our daily bread. / Johnny Hall's mother had nothing to give him for supper. He prayed that line with her, and a gentleman came asking her to keep his two motherless boys. - Matthew 6:11
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Give Us This Day Our Daily Bread."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
In the spring of 1872 a missionary, his wife, and their child were in Cadereita, Mexico, asking God for a way back to the States for a little season. About the middle of March the means came, but the country was in revolution and no stages were running. They hired two men with Mexican carts, one for themselves and a mattress, one for baggage and provisions, through mostly uncultivated country.

They knew General Cortinas and his troops were somewhere between them and Texas. The account says that when they met him he treated them with courtesy, bid them good morning, and rode on without examining their baggage.

In Brownsville, Texas, people who heard it said they could not have believed Cortinas capable of such kindness to Americans so entirely in his power. The missionary and his wife believed God had restrained the man, in answer to prayer.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: NO STAGES WERE RUNNING. THEY TOOK MEXICAN CARTS TOWARD TEXAS. CORTINAS WAS OUT.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Prayer of a Missionary in Mexico Answered.--Saved from Banditti."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 4, "The All-Prevailing Plea," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"O LORD God! the Fountain of all fullness, we, who are nothing but emptiness, come unto Thee for all supplies, nor shall we come in vain, since we bear with us a plea which is all prevalent. Since we come commanded by Thy Word, encouraged by Thy promise, and preceded by Christ Jesus, our great High Priest, we know that whatsoever we shall ask in prayer, believing, we shall receive. Only do Thou help us now to ask right things and may the utterances of our mouth be acceptable in Thy sight, O God our Strength and our Redeemer."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: O LORD GOD! THE FOUNTAIN OF ALL FULLNESS
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 67:

"We have cast off fear, and restrained prayer before God; have not called upon thy name, nor stirred up ourselves to take hold on thee."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Where have we restrained prayer?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 67. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A Brooklyn home missionary heard this from a Christian friend who kept a restaurant. The man had cleared a large sum one day, part of it in Mexican dollars. On the way home he thought of the widow of a dear friend, whom he knew to be in want. He told himself he would go tomorrow. He still could not sleep. Something kept saying go now. It was not far from eleven when he dressed and went.

A dim light was in her upper room. The door was ajar and he heard her praying. He had a few of the Mexican dollars in his pocket. He pushed the door just wide enough and rolled the pieces in along the carpet, then left.

She rose from her knees and saw the silver on the floor. She did not know how it had come. She knew it was from the Lord. Later, at a prayer meeting, she told it. The restaurant keeper was there and said the dollars had come from the Lord, and that he had been sent to carry them. A later note in the book says she owed a sum she had to pay at once, and had been pleading that night for that amount.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: AT ELEVEN HE COULD NOT SLEEP. HE ROLLED THE DOLLARS UNDER HER DOOR.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Widow In "Want"."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Someone held an open letter, an invitation to visit friends she had never seen. She wanted to go, and then she could not see where the money or the proper clothing would come from. Weeks passed. She wrote that she could not come at present, but she could not give it up in her heart. Her parents were visiting in the far West. Night after night in her little room she told the Lord about it.

One day her brother-in-law said he would pay her expenses to and fro. She kept praying. The account says the way opened, and that the sense of being led stayed with her through the visit. When she visited that home again the next winter, it came back.

The book sets the story under the words, "I will hold thee by thy right hand, saying unto thee, fear not, I will help thee."
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE LETTER SAID COME. SHE WROTE BACK THAT SHE COULD NOT. SHE KEPT PRAYING.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Visit To Friends."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 5, "To The King Eternal," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR God and Father, draw us to Thyself by Thy Spirit and may the few minutes that we spend in prayer be full of the true spirit of supplication. Grant that none of us with closed eyes may yet be looking abroad over the fields of vanity, but may our eyes be really shut to everything else now but that which is spiritual and divine. May we have communion with God in the secret of our hearts and find Him to be to us as a little sanctuary."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR GOD AND FATHER, DRAW US TO THYSELF BY THY SPIRIT
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A clergyman wrote The Christian that in the winter of 1872 he was in missionary work in new fields, with his wife, without a pledged salary. Debts for the necessaries of life had piled up. He felt impressed to pray for fifty dollars, and he told his wife so. She said she would join him. They asked for fifty dollars so they would not bring themselves or the truth they preached into reproach.

The money came. He wrote that if he ever recognized the hand of God in anything, he did in this, and that it was easier to trust afterward. He quoted, "I will never leave thee nor forsake thee," and the line about making requests known to God with thanksgiving.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE TOLD HIS WIFE HE WAS GOING TO PRAY FOR FIFTY DOLLARS. SHE SAID SHE WOULD JOIN HIM.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Prayer For Fifty Dollars."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 75:

"We have known our Master's will, but have not done it, and therefore deserve to be beaten with many stripes."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: What have we known and not done?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 75. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
D. L. Moody told of a young man from his native village. They were working on a farm together one day and the man was weeping. When he left home his mother had given him the text, "Seek ye first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you." He wanted to get rich first, and give his attention to religion when he was comfortable. He went from village to village and found nothing to do.

Moody said that years later he found the man at home, rocking in his chair, and the man pointed at him and said, "Young man, seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness." Moody had just laid his younger brother in the grave, a few yards from that man, and he asked the people listening to seek the kingdom now.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HIS MOTHER GAVE HIM ONE TEXT. HE SAID HE WOULD SEEK GOD AFTER HE WAS COMFORTABLE.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("One Who Refused The Holy Spirit."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
On November 22, 1873, the French steamship Ville du Havre, bound from New York to France, was sunk in a collision with the Loch Earn. About two hundred passengers went down with her. The rest were taken up by the Loch Earn. Most were later transferred to the Trimountain. Some stayed on the disabled Loch Earn and seemed in danger again.

On December 11, while D. L. Moody was leading a noonday prayer meeting in Edinburgh, Dr. Andrew Thompson read a letter from a Christian lady, the mother of one of those still at risk. The account says a ship saw their signal of distress. After they were taken aboard the pilot boat that brought them into Plymouth, Mr. Cook read them the account of Paul's shipwreck and asked what made that captain change his course against his will, if not the ever present Spirit of God.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE VILLE DU HAVRE WENT DOWN. A MOTHER IN EDINBURGH WAS STILL PRAYING.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Rescue from the Ville du Havre, and the Loch Earn."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 6, "The Wonders of Calvary," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"GREAT God, there was a time when we dreaded the thought of coming near to Thee, for we were guilty and Thou wast angry with us, but now we will praise Thee because Thine anger is turned away and Thou comfortest us. Ay, and the very throne which once was a place of dread has now become the place of shelter. I flee unto Thee to hide me."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: GREAT GOD, THERE WAS A TIME WHEN WE DREADED THE THOUGHT OF COMING NEAR TO THEE,
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
An unbelieving father came home and asked where his little girl was. His wife said she had gone to bed. He went to give her one kiss. At the bedroom door he heard her praying, "Do, God Almighty, please lead daddy to hear Mr. Stowell preach."

She had often asked him to go, and he had always said no. After he heard that prayer, he decided that the next time she asked, he would go. He went, and the sermon pricked his conscience. Leaving the church, he took her hand and said, "Jane, thy God shall be my God, and thy minister shall be my minister." The book says he became a true follower of the Lord.

The same bank entry continues into a separate anecdote.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE WENT IN TO KISS HIS LITTLE GIRL. SHE WAS ASKING GOD TO BRING HIM TO CHURCH.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Unbelieving Father led to go to Church."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 86:

"But we must not think in our prayers to prescribe to Him, or by our importunity to move Him."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Are we trying to write his answer for him?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 86. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: A crippled orphan boy knelt by a stump in the woods outside a depot in August 1874. He needed to get to Lowell and had been refused a ride. A man who heard him pray put five dollars in his hand.
Alt text(s): Image reading: My God shall supply all your need. / A crippled orphan boy knelt by a stump in the woods outside a depot in August 1874. He needed to get to Lowell and had been refused a ride. A man who heard him pray put five dollars in his hand. - Philippians 4:19
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Prayer In The Woods."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
In a northern city a Christian and an infidel went to law. The infidel sued for a heavy sum, saying the Christian had promised to pay it for stocks. The Christian said there had been an offer, and that he had steadily refused any trade. Each man had a friend who backed him.

The judge told the jurors it was a grave task: one of the parties must be guilty of deliberate perjury, because the stories could not both be true. The Christian had asked God to vindicate him.

The jury's foreman said he felt the truth must be with the defendant, and asked what the others said. Every hand went up. They acquitted him. He gave thanks with a new confidence in the line, "Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me."
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE JUDGE TOLD THE JURY THAT ONE OF THE TWO MEN HAD TO BE LYING.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Remarkable Decision By A Jury."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 7, "“Let All the People Praise Thee”," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR Father, when we read Thy description of human nature we are sure it is true, for Thou has seen man ever since his fall and Thou hast been grieved at heart concerning him. Moreover, Thou hast such a love towards him that Thou didst not judge him harshly and every word that Thou hast spoken must be according to truth. Thou hast measured and computed the iniquity of man, for Thou hast laid it on the Well-Beloved and we know Thou hast not laid upon Him more than is meet."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR FATHER, WHEN WE READ THY DESCRIPTION OF HUMAN NATURE WE ARE SURE IT IS TRUE,
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 94:

"Though we are no more worthy to be called thy children; for how shouldest thou put us that have been rebellious among the children, and give us the pleasant land?"
Alt text(s): Question card reading: What would we ask if we remembered we are not worthy?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 94. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A city missionary, going home on a Saturday night with a basket of provisions, asked a policeman whether any families had moved onto his beat that week. The officer pointed up an alley. A woman and some children were living there.

He went in. She was sewing by a small light. Two little girls, about nine to twelve, were playing in the corner. He asked if they might come to Sunday school in the morning. She said she would allow it, but what they had on was all the clothing they had. He said, "The Lord will provide," and asked if she had any money. She said not yet, but that she had committed her case to the Lord.

The next morning he found money he believed had been cast in his way, and though it was the Sabbath he went to a neighborhood baker, told him the circumstances, and bought bread. The baker added a bountiful supply. The missionary wrote that from that hour, for nearly fifty years, he never doubted that God would take care of his children.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE GIRLS HAD NOTHING TO WEAR TO SUNDAY SCHOOL BUT WHAT WAS ALREADY ON THEM.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Lord Will Provide."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
The Christian told of a minister in Ohio who in 1860 supplied a congregation still a whole year behind on their former pastor's salary. They could promise him only five dollars a Sunday until that debt was paid. At the end of the year only about two-thirds of even that had come. His periodicals alone had cost sixteen dollars, and he could not stop them without paying the arrears.

On New Year's Day he married a couple and gave his wife the five-dollar fee for a dress. She had admired a certain cloth. Instead of buying it, she wrote a letter that put the five dollars to another use. The Board of Missions later sent her own letter back in print and asked if she had written it. If so, a man in New York had authorized twenty-five dollars, with the request that she buy a dress worth five dollars and give the rest to her husband and children. Her five dollars came back, with four times as much added.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE FEE WAS FIVE DOLLARS, FOR A DRESS. SHE SENT THE FIVE DOLLARS AWAY.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Compound Interest."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 8, "A Prayer for Holiness," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR Father, we worship and love Thee and it is one point of our worship that Thou art holy. Time was when we loved Thee for Thy mercy. We knew no more, but now Thou hast changed our hearts and made us in love with goodness, purity, justice, true holiness, and we understand now why “the cherubim and seraphim continually do cry, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts.” We adore Thee because Thou art holy and we love Thee for Thine infinite perfection. For now, we sigh and cry after holiness ourselves. Sanctify us wholly, spirit, soul, and body."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR FATHER, WE WORSHIP AND LOVE THEE
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
About July 30, 1864, Confederate troops invaded and pillaged Chambersburg. A Sabbath-school superintendent who had fled the South because of his loyalty to the national government left at gray dawn with his wife and two little girls for the mountains northwest of the town. He knew what discovery would cost him.

After days and nights under the trees, with no food, they were nearly famished. He went off by himself, his back against a large oak, because he could not watch them starve. His eldest daughter, not quite ten, found him. She had brought her little Testament. She read Matthew 6:9 and following, through "give us this day our daily bread," and asked whether the Saviour who taught his disciples to pray for bread would let them starve.

He prayed the Lord's Prayer with her. He had scarcely finished when a small dog ran up and barked until its owner came, a farmer searching the mountain for cattle he had lost for several days. The farmer took the family to his house and provided for them.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THEY HAD FLED THE TOWN WITH NO FOOD. HIS DAUGHTER READ HIM GIVE US THIS DAY.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Child's Faith In The Lord's Prayer."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 102:

"Teach us thy way, O God, and lead us in a plain path, because of our observers."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Who is watching the path we ask him to make plain?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 102. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A merchant of St. Petersburg supported several native missionaries in India at his own cost, and gave liberally at home. Asked how he could afford it, he said that before his conversion he had served the world and himself on a grand scale. When God called him, he resolved that Christ and his cause should have more than he had ever spent on the world.

He promised to give a fixed proportion of all his business brought in. Every year since, he said, the business had brought in about double what it did the year before, so that he could double his gifts.

The book sets John Bunyan's lines beside that answer.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE ASKED HOW THE MERCHANT COULD AFFORD THE MISSIONARIES. THE MAN TOLD HIM THE RULE.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Giving Blessed."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A minister looked out while it was still dark and saw a woman of his church weeping at the gate. Her husband, one of the bitterest Universalists he knew, had ridden away and said he would not come back until the religious flurry was over.

The minister told her they would lay the case before the Lord and ask that the man be brought back under the power of the Spirit. At the crowded meeting he stated it: the husband had fled into the country, and they were to pray the Spirit would follow him.

That evening the same man walked into the prayer meeting. He said he had ridden over the hills, back from the river, eighteen miles, and on the top of a hill had been stopped as suddenly as Paul. He said he had lost his Universalism and knew he must be born again. The book says he later became an elder in a Presbyterian church, and that he believed he was converted in that prayer meeting.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE RODE EIGHTEEN MILES TO GET AWAY FROM THE MEETINGS. HE CAME BACK THE SAME DAY.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("He Could Not Flee from the Power of the Holy Spirit."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 9, "Glorious Liberty," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR Father, we bless Thy name that we can say from the bottom of our hearts, “Abba, Father.” It is the chief joy of our lives that we have become the children of God by faith which is in Christ Jesus and we can in the deep calm of our spirit say, “Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be Thy name, Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth as in heaven.” Lord, we thank Thee for the liberty which comes to our emancipated spirit through the adoption which Thou hast made us to enjoy."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR FATHER, WE BLESS THY NAME THAT WE CAN SAY FROM THE BOTTOM OF OUR HEARTS,
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Rev. Mr. H. said a friend gave him a five-dollar gold piece when gold was scarce. He resolved not to spend it, and carried it a long time as a token of friendship.

Riding in the country, he met an acquaintance with a subscription book for a church in a destitute place. He said he could do nothing, that his pocket was empty. The man excused him and they parted.

Down the road he remembered the gold in his vest pocket. He had told the man he had no money while the piece was on him the whole time. He turned back. The book records that he treated the untruth as something he had to undo.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE SAID HIS POCKET WAS EMPTY. THEN HE REMEMBERED THE GOLD HE HAD SWORN NOT TO SPEND.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Five-Dollar Gold Piece."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 110:

"Though bonds and afflictions should abide us, Lord, grant that none of these things may move us, and that we may not count life itself dear to us, so we may finish our course with joy."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: What are we counting dearer than finishing the course?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 110. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: A pastor fasting over a decision heard a knock while he was still asking. His mother-in-law said two gentlemen were already in the parlor. He had not sent for them.
Alt text(s): Image reading: Before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear. / A pastor fasting over a decision heard a knock while he was still asking. His mother-in-law said two gentlemen were already in the parlor. He had not sent for them. - Isaiah 65:24
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Before They Call I Will Answer."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
When Samuel Harris of Virginia began to preach, he neglected the work of the farm. He needed more grain than he had raised, and he called on a man who owed him. The man said he had no money. Harris said he would take wheat, at the current price, because the man had raised a good crop. The man said he had other uses for the wheat. Asked how he intended to pay, he said he never intended to pay until he was sued, and Harris might begin the suit as soon as he pleased.

Harris would not sue.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE MAN SAID, SUE ME. HARRIS HAD GONE TO HIM FOR WHEAT FOR HIS FAMILY.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Samuel Harris's Lawsuit, and How the Lord Settled it for Him."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 10, "The Music of Praise," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"O THOU blessed God, we must be helped of Thy Spirit or we cannot worship Thee aright. Behold the holy angels adore Thee and the hosts redeemed by blood bring everlasting Hallelujahs to Thy feet. What are we, the creatures of a day, polluted with sin, that we should think that we can praise thee? And yet the music of praise were not complete if Thy children did not join in it, even those of them who are still in this world below. Help us, then, enable us to tune our harps and to fetch forth music from our spirit.."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: O THOU BLESSED GOD, WE MUST BE HELPED OF THY SPIRIT
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 121:

"Let our souls bless the Lord, and let all that is within us bless his holy name; yea, let our souls bless the Lord, and not forget any of his benefits."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Which benefit have we already forgotten?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 121. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A correspondent of The Guiding Hand went to the city of R. to see his brother. The firm where the brother had worked had suspended. He had broken up housekeeping. All anyone knew was that he was boarding somewhere in the suburbs. The visitor searched all day and did not find him.

He wrote a line, dropped it in the post office, and asked the Lord to send his brother there to get it. The note said to meet him at a stated place at ten the next morning. At ten the brother came.

On the way home the brother said he had arranged to go fishing on the bay early that morning. When he woke he had such an impression to go to the post office that he gave up the bay and went.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE SEARCHED THE CITY ALL DAY. THEN HE DROPPED A LINE IN THE POST OFFICE.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Go To The Post-Office."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A clergyman in New York was turned out of his pulpit through a disaffected member, and a large family was left in necessity. At supper he watched the last morsel of bread put on the table, with nothing in sight for breakfast. His wife and children went to bed. He sat up with the promises.

In the morning, in the depth of winter, with a little fire on the hearth, he asked his wife to hang on the kettle and spread the cloth. The kettle boiled. The children cried for bread. The account says supply came to that table. He had chosen to set it as if the answer were already on the way.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE LAST MORSEL WAS ON THE TABLE. HE TOLD HIS WIFE TO HANG THE KETTLE ON.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Help at the Very Last Moment. Faith Rewarded."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 12, "On Holy Ground," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be Thy name, Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” We fear that we often begin our prayer with petitions for ourselves and put our daily bread before Thy kingdom and the pardoning of our sins before the hallowing of Thy name. We would not do so today, but guided by our Lord’s model of prayer, we would first pray for Thy glory and here, great God, we would adore Thee. Thou hast made us and not we ourselves."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR FATHER, WHICH ART IN HEAVEN, HALLOWED BE THY NAME, THY KINGDOM COME
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Mrs. Jarvis laid English blankets in a box the ladies of the church were filling for the poor, and said they must be very poor who have nothing to give. Then she told them she had once been very poor.

A missionary lectured in her village. She had no decent apparel, so she slipped in late and sat behind the door. When the pastor asked the congregation to fill a box for his return, she wanted to send something. At home her children were asleep and her husband, long out of work, was waiting up. She looked over her clothes and the children's and found nothing she could spare except two brown towels.

The next day she pieced out the best one, and after dark slipped it into the box. She told the ladies it was not long after that her husband got a good situation, and that she dated their prosperity from the brown towel.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE RICH WOMAN SAID SHE HAD ONCE HAD NOTHING TO GIVE BUT A BROWN TOWEL.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Brown Towel."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 129:

"Thine they were, and thou gavest them to Christ, and this is thy will, that of all that thou hast given him he should lose nothing, but should raise it up at the last day."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Whom are we afraid he will lose?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 129. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A ship was overtaken in a long storm. The captain was a Christian, and the crew was obedient, but the ship was too badly strained. The leaks were beyond the pumps. He committed them to God and made ready for the boats. A sail was sighted, drawn by their signals, and everyone was taken off. They watched their own ship go down.

The ship that had rescued them was then caught in a dreadful storm of its own and thrown on her beam ends. The book sets the story under the idea that the men had prayed in fair weather, before they needed the prayer.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THEY WERE ALREADY SAFE ON THE OTHER SHIP WHEN THE SECOND STORM HIT.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Praying In Fair Weather."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Returning from the north country, a man saw small debts to be paid, and the hand of God seemed fast closed. A special debt of twenty pounds hung a long time. He wrote that he chalked out roads for the Almighty to walk in, and no raven came, morning or evening.

A gentlewoman was visiting. He asked if she had twenty pounds in her pocket, and told her how much he wanted it. She said she had not, or he should have had it. A few hours later she came to his study, found it locked, and knocked. He let her in.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: TWENTY POUNDS HAD HUNG A LONG TIME. HE ASKED A GUEST IF SHE HAD IT IN HER POCKET.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Lord Paid His Debt."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 13, "The Wings of Prayer," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR Father, Thy children who know Thee delight themselves in Thy presence. We are never happier than when we are near Thee. We have found a little heaven in prayer. It has eased our load to tell Thee of its weight. It has relieved our wound to tell Thee of its smart. It has restored our spirit to confess to Thee its wanderings. No place like the Mercy Seat for us. We thank Thee, Lord, that we have not only found benefit in prayer, but in the answers to it, we have been greatly enriched."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR FATHER, THY CHILDREN WHO KNOW THEE DELIGHT THEMSELVES IN THY PRESENCE
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
The writer said he was taught early that God cares about little daily wants. At about ten he gave five cents each Sabbath for foreign missions. The money was not handed to him. He earned it on errands, outside his chores.

When he was walking a mile to school, the walk and the farm chores left him no way to earn anything for some months. One Sabbath he dropped his last silver piece into the collection, knowing the next Sunday he would have none.

He carried that empty Sunday to God the way he had been taught to carry smaller wants.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HIS LAST FIVE CENTS WENT INTO THE MISSION BOX. THE NEXT SUNDAY HE HAD NONE.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("God's Care for Little Children in Little Wants."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 149:

"O let thy salvation and thy righteousness be openly shewed in the sight of the heathen, and let all the ends of the earth see the salvation of our God."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Where do we still want his salvation kept private?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 149. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: William Huntington, in The Bank of Faith, answered people who said we have no warrant to pray for temporal blessings by pointing at that promise. He had watched daily bread arrive for the poor.
Alt text(s): Image reading: Godliness has promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come. / William Huntington, in The Bank of Faith, answered people who said we have no warrant to pray for temporal blessings by pointing at that promise. He had watched daily bread arrive for the poor. - 1 Timothy 4:8
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Bank Of Faith. God The Guardian Of The Poor."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Mr. Huntington, unable to provide for his family and depending only on God, wrote that as he went over a bridge he saw a very large eel on the mud, apparently dead. It was only asleep. He got it onto the grass and carried it home. His little one was fond of it, and it supplied her that day. By night the eel was gone, and the next day the same distress returned.

The next morning, as he entered the garden gate, he saw a partridge lying dead. The book sets both beside Elijah fed by a raven.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE SAW AN EEL ASLEEP IN THE MUD. IT FED HIS LITTLE ONE FOR THAT DAY.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The God who Supplied Elijah by a Raven Supplied me with Fish."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 14, "“Bless The Lord, O My Soul!”," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"LORD, we are longing to draw near, may Thy Spirit draw us near. We come by the way of Christ our Mediator. We could not approach Thee, O our God, if it were not for Him, but in Him we come boldly to the throne of heavenly grace. Nor can we come without thanksgiving—thanksgiving from the heart, such as the tongue can never express. Thou hast chosen us from before the foundation of the world and this well-head of mercy sends forth streams of loving-kindness never ceasing. Because we were chosen, we have been redeemed with precious blood."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: LORD, WE ARE LONGING TO DRAW NEAR, MAY THY SPIRIT DRAW US NEAR
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 158:

"O send from above, and deliver them from those that hate them, and bring them forth into a large place."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Who needs to be brought into a large place?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 158. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Their father went abroad after selling one of their two cows and taking the money. The account calls him a reckless spendthrift, fond of the public inn. A rich neighbor offered to lend enough to buy another cow. They accepted.

In summer they could sell fourteen measures of milk, in winter twelve, and the borrowed money was soon paid. The cow also did the farm work with a strength that astonished them. When the father came home and heard them praise the animal, he was enraged and offered it at half its value.

The children were afraid they would lose it whenever anyone came near. Their mother said that if their father could always do as he liked, none of them would be alive, but God would not let him go farther than was for their good, and would keep the cow as long as they needed it. The cow never left while she was alive. When the children were provided for, a purchaser came.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THEIR FATHER SOLD ONE COW AND LEFT. THEIR MOTHER SAID GOD WOULD KEEP THE OTHER.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Buying A Cow."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A sailor lived a profligate life. His mother followed him into drinking saloons and gambling houses. At last he stayed away from home whenever he was in port. She knelt and cast the burden on the Lord, and felt a strong conviction that she was answered.

For several years he went on, and she sorrowed, but the fear had lifted. Then for several years she heard nothing and thought him dead. She stopped praying for his conversion and held on to meeting him in heaven.

He came home at last, only thirty, broken down by dissipation and hardship, still unconverted. To satisfy her, he stayed in the room while the district missionary visited. The missionary did not begin with wrath. He spoke of the love of Jesus that waits longer than any earthly friend. The young man listened at first with indifference.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE FOLLOWED HIM INTO THE SALOONS. THEN FOR YEARS SHE HEARD NOTHING.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("His Mother's Prayer."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 15, "The Peace of God," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR God, we stand not afar off as Israel did in Sinai, nor does a veil hang dark between Thy face and ours, but the veil is rent by the death of our divine Lord and Mediator, Jesus Christ, and in His name we come up to the Mercy Seat all blood besprinkled, and here we present our prayers and our praises accepted in Him."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR GOD, WE STAND NOT AFAR OFF AS ISRAEL DID IN SINAI
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A contributor to The Christian lost a pocketbook with money and papers of a large amount, about what he was owing. He had been a mile and a half from home. He did not know it was gone until about nine in the evening. His health was poor, and the road was so dark he thought he could not find it that night. He decided to stay awake and start searching at three in the morning, before anyone else passed.

He also prayed.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE LOST THE POCKETBOOK A MILE AND A HALF FROM HOME. HE PLANNED TO SEARCH AT THREE.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Praying for a Lost Pocket-Book."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 175:

"The day is thine, the night also is thine, thou hast prepared the light and the sun."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: If the night is his, why are we afraid of it?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 175. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A man who had led a wicked life was converted. Before that, a debt of $18.75 had not troubled him. Afterward he heard the command, "Pay what thou owest." He asked his creditor to take a bureau, a table, and a looking-glass and sell them for the debt. The creditor would not take the furniture out of the house, and said he would wait. They set November 18.

The night of the 17th the man prayed until daybreak and rose sure that he would be delivered. The next morning, on his way to business, a storekeeper stopped him. The book says the incident came to both the storekeeper and the creditor as evidence of God's presence.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: AFTER HE WAS CONVERTED, A DEBT OF $18.75 WOULD NOT LET HIM ALONE.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("That $18.75."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
About eight years before he wrote, a college student was embarrassed for funds. Debts accumulated. He had promised to pay on a date, expecting money from the usual sources. It did not come.

He locked the study door and sat down. He saw an auction of his few books and scanty furniture, then notes and protests. Then the promises came to mind. "All things whatsoever ye have need of" came home with power. He had given up business to preach. He asked for help and at last felt confident.

A letter arrived by way of a broker in H., who mentioned his name. It asked for a peculiar legal service, contained money, and promised more. Over three times the sum he had asked was finally given, more than enough for a term's expenses. He never mentioned the need, or the prayer, to anyone at the time.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE MONEY HE HAD COUNTED ON DID NOT COME. HE LOCKED THE STUDY DOOR.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("All Our Needs."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 16, "He Ever Liveth," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR God, we come to Thee by Jesus Christ who has gone within the veil on our behalf and ever liveth to make intercession for us. Our poor prayers could never reach Thee were it not for Him, but His hands are full of sweet perfume which makes our pleading sweet with Thee. His blood is sprinkled on the Mercy Seat and now we know that Thou dost always hear those who approach Thee through that ever blessed name. We have deeply felt our entire unworthiness even to lift up our eyes to the place where Thine honor dwelleth."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR GOD, WE COME TO THEE BY JESUS CHRIST
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A New York tradesman pledged a certain portion of his receipts to the Lord as fast as they were collected. He called it the Lord's insurance money. As long as he gave, he said, the Lord would help him, and in some way give him the means to give. It was no money lost. It kept his heart open, and it was the surest way he knew to keep the Lord's favor.

He said he had never realized before how closely the Lord was connected with his business. Bad debts he had not expected were paid. When he stopped giving, business stopped coming. When he stopped praying for the business, perplexities rose. As long as he prayed, it moved easily. He called the Lord his banker, his insurer, and his deliverer in temporal things as well as spiritual.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE CALLED A PORTION OF EVERY RECEIPT THE LORD'S INSURANCE MONEY.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Lord's Insurance Money."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 184:

"O give us grace to worship thee with reverence and godly fear, because thou our God art a consuming fire."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Do we worship a God we think we can manage?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 184. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: A missionary on a tenement's third floor read that verse to an English wife whose husband was in a cell as a vagrant. On the day of release the husband said the Spirit had met him in the cell. Within months they joined a church and taught Sunday school.
Alt text(s): Image reading: For thy Maker is thine husband; the Lord of hosts is his name. / A missionary on a tenement's third floor read that verse to an English wife whose husband was in a cell as a vagrant. On the day of release the husband said the Spirit had met him in the cell. Within months they joined a church and taught Sunday school. - Isaiah 54:5
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Prisoner Loosed."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A New York business man had several large amounts coming due. Tradesmen asked to be paid sooner than usual and drained him. His receipts fell to half. A bank loan, a mortgage, and large notes were all in front of him. He asked the Lord either to send business or to open a way, and he went back to his trade.

When the bank loan fell due, he was surprised to learn that a trifling payment would be accepted and the rest extended. The security had not improved in any way he could see. Within three months a way opened to clear the rest of the mortgage before it was due.

The book says the Lord relieved him, eased his creditors, and gave him profitable ways of trade. It adds that business needs prayer as much as the home and the church.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: RECEIPTS FELL BY HALF. A LOAN, A MORTGAGE, AND THE NOTES WERE ALL DUE.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Help In Paying A Mortgage."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 17, "To Be Like Christ," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"BLESSED art Thou, O God, teach us Thy statutes! Because Thou art the infinitely blessed One, Thou canst impart blessing, and Thou art infinitely willing to do so, and therefore do we approach Thee with great confidence, through Jesus Christ Thy Son, whom Thou hast made blessed forevermore. Oh! hear Thou the voice of Thy servants this day and according to Thine infinite love and wisdom answer Thou us, according to Thy riches in glory, by Christ Jesus. First we would confess before Thee, O God, the sin we have committed, mourning over it."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: BLESSED ART THOU, O GOD, TEACH US THY STATUTES! BECAUSE THOU ART THE INFINITELY BLESSED ONE,
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 192:

"Give to those who are ordained to take heed to the ministry which they have received of the Lord, that they fulfil it, and to make full proof of it by watching in all things."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Who is watching over us in the ministry?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 192. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Dr. Patton of Chicago received a letter from Mr. F., a pastor in Massachusetts. The pastor had lost a knife he prized, a present from a friend, on a hillside covered with laurels. He stopped and prayed to be guided, began to search, and was almost immediately successful.

The same letter tells of a friend in a responsible government post whose accounts would not balance. After a long search he could not find the error. He prayed, opened the books, and on the first page he happened to glance at, at the top of the column, the error stood out so plainly he wondered he had missed it.

Another man in the same letter said his spending money came to about fifty cents a year. He rose, looked at the ground, and without planning a course walked across a meadow to near the farther edge. The penknife was in the grass directly in front of him. Ten feet to either side, the grass was too high for him to have seen it.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE LOST A KNIFE ON A HILLSIDE OF LAUREL. HE PRAYED, THEN WALKED STRAIGHT TO IT.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Help Of The Lord In Little Things."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A London correspondent of the Western Christian Advocate wrote about a fund to extinguish debts on chapels. A gentleman named Wilkes, who had promised a thousand guineas to that fund, had been a journeyman mechanic seven years earlier. He invented and patented a crank or spindle used in cotton manufacture, and he needed capital. He prayed to be directed to someone able and willing to help.

In a way he had not arranged, an elderly Quaker, a stranger, accosted him: "Friend, I should like to know if a little money would be of any service to thee." The stranger satisfied himself and backed him.

By 1853 Wilkes was giving seven guineas daily to that cause, upwards of $10,500 a year, besides the thousand guineas. The writer added that he kept the utmost simplicity.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SEVEN YEARS BEFORE, HE WAS A JOURNEYMAN. IN 1853 HE WAS GIVING SEVEN GUINEAS A DAY.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Prosperity And Liberality."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 18, "O, For More Grace!," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR Father, Thou dost hear us when we pray. Thou hast provided an advocate and intercessor in heaven now. We cannot come to Thee unless Thy Holy Spirit shall suggest desire and help us while we plead. We would ask that the subject which caused such conflict to Paul may be beyond conflict with us. May we know the Christ and have Him to be our all in all. We would have the conflict about others, but may we be past it for ourselves. He is everything to us, more than all in Him we find."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR FATHER, THOU DOST HEAR US WHEN WE PRAY
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
On New Year's Day the writer set out to visit poorer neighbors and meant to take a sovereign to a widow who had once known comfort. The drawer for the poor held only that one sovereign, and the allowance was not due for two or three weeks. She nearly closed the drawer. Then 2 Chronicles 25:9 came to mind: "The Lord is able to give thee much more than this." She took the sovereign.

The widow's tears ran down her cheeks. She took the visitor's hands and asked the God of the widow and the fatherless to bless her.

Before the day closed, a comparative stranger wrote that many poor would be claiming help, and asked her to dispense the enclosed five pounds as she saw fit. A box of soap worth four pounds was ordered for the same purpose. Nine times what she had given came in before the day ended.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE HAD ONE SOVEREIGN LEFT FOR THE POOR. THE VERSE MADE HER GIVE THAT ONE.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A New Year's Incident."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 200:

"In love to their souls deliver them from the pit of corruption, and cast all their sins behind thy back."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Whose sins are we still holding in front of him?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 200. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
During the New York draft riots of the Civil War, on the first day of the mob, several thousand people with clubs and brickbats appeared at the Colored Orphan Asylum and broke down the front door with an axe. The building was fired in ten or fifteen places and destroyed in about twenty minutes.

Two hundred and twenty-three children were inside with their attendants and teachers. The matron gathered the children. A teacher asked them whether they believed God could take care of them, and they went out through the halls. One teacher said she would never forget the silence, the tears, and the yells getting nearer.

Not one of the children was injured. They passed through the rioters and were removed to a place of safety. The book calls it an answer to the prayer offered in the building.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE MOB BROKE IN THE DOOR OF THE COLORED ORPHAN ASYLUM. NOT ONE CHILD WAS HURT.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Extraordinary Care of the Lord in Answer to Prayer."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A merchant said that when he consecrated his life anew, he knew riches could ensnare him, so he decided his plan of giving before wealth could bias him. Every month he balanced the accounts as nearly as he could, reserved enough of the profits to cover probable losses, and entered one tenth of the rest on a benevolent account. He and his family lived on the other nine tenths.

If net profits, after clerk hire and store expenses, passed $500 in a month, he gave twelve and a half percent. Over $700, fifteen percent. Over $900, he went higher still, on the scale he had set before the money arrived.

He wrote that he prospered beyond his expectations. Though he was constantly giving, he had never touched the bottom of the fund. Some months the tenth left too little to live on. The tide turned, and he recognized a heavenly hand making good the past deficiencies.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE LAID ASIDE A TENTH BEFORE THE BOOKS COULD ARGUE HIM OUT OF IT.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Dividing With God."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 19, "God’s Unspeakable Gift," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"O LORD, many of us feel like the lame man at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. Come by this way and make the lame ones perfectly sound. O Lord, Thou canst do by Thy servants today what Thou didst by them in the olden time. Work miracles of mercy even upon outer court worshippers who are too lame to get into the holy place. But there are many who feel like that man when he was restored. We would follow our Restorer, the Prince of Life, into the temple, leaping and walking and praising God."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: O LORD, MANY OF US FEEL LIKE THE LAME MAN
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
The writer said that after other needs had been met, they could not find suitable help in the house. Before he started out one morning he prayed in secret to be directed, and he kept praying as he called at different places. He soon found a colored woman who came to work for them.

She lived in the family a year and a half, taught two of the children to read, and was glad to move with them until she left to be married. The account says she later fell sick and died. That is not told as a cure. It is told as the end of a helper who had come when they prayed for one. The writer adds that a dozen other times, in straits, prayer procured the help they needed.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: BEFORE HE LEFT THE HOUSE HE ASKED TO BE LED TO THE RIGHT HELP.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Prayer For A Servant."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 208:

"Jacob wrestles with the angel; but he must go, for the day breaks: We must therefore think of concluding."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: What are we still wrestling for after the day has broken?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 208. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: In January 1863 a Connecticut woman, alone with two little boys while her husband was in the army, could not buy a quarter-cord of wood. She wrote that Abraham could say on Moriah, "The Lord will provide," and that every stick in her shed seemed to say Jehovah-Jireh.
Alt text(s): Image reading: Jehovah-Jireh. The Lord will provide. / In January 1863 a Connecticut woman, alone with two little boys while her husband was in the army, could not buy a quarter-cord of wood. She later pointed to the pile in the shed and said the Lord does provide. - Genesis 22:14
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Prayer For A Load Of Wood."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
In a frame dwelling in a Brooklyn alley, two rooms on the first floor, an old colored man who had fought life for ninety years lay in the smaller room. Fifteen of those years he had been on his bed, his eyes too dim to read. His wife was eye and ear and comfort to him. Both were earnest Christians.

She had been brought up in the West Indies as a Catholic, and her religion had been mostly counting beads. In Brooklyn she became a servant in the family of a naval officer. A young painter working in the house, a Christian whose light showed at home, spoke to her and invited her to a prayer meeting.

He was still on the bed. The story is that she came to trust Christ in a way the rosary had never given her.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE HAD COUNTED BEADS. A PAINTER IN THE HOUSE ASKED HER TO A PRAYER MEETING.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Wonderful Conversion Of A Roman Catholic."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 20, "The Great Sacrifice," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"O GOD our Father, we do remember well when we were called to Thee, with many sweet and wooing voices we were bidden to return. Thou didst Thyself hang out the lights of mercy that we might know the way home and Thy dear Son Himself came down to seek us. But we wandered still."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: O GOD OUR FATHER, WE DO REMEMBER WELL WHEN WE WERE CALLED TO THEE
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 220:

"Thou art the Father of our spirits, to whom we ought to be in subjection and live."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: If he is the Father of our spirits, what are we still ruling ourselves?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 220. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
In a cottage in Connecticut two sisters were caring for a brother who had been on a bed of sickness for many months. The younger sister grew discouraged. She was dependent on the home. She said she would go away and work and earn money.

Her mother said she knew the girl needed shoes, and told her not to worry, the Lord would provide. The younger sister asked whether she thought the Lord would come down from heaven and buy her a pair of shoes.

The need the girl named, and the need her mother handed to the Lord, was the pair of shoes.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE ASKED IF THE LORD WOULD COME DOWN AND BUY HER THE SHOES.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Pair of Shoes.--The Lord's Rebuke to those who "Didn't Believe."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
At the Consumptive's Home, three thousand dollars in the safe, reserved for a payment on a new building, was stolen. Not a dollar was left.

They pleaded John 15:7, "If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you," and they asked for the three thousand dollars. A promise was made that the amount would be paid out on a certain day.

Before that day arrived, the Lord had sent the three thousand dollars in unusual contributions. Both the Lord's promise and the children's promise were kept. The book says an ordinary business man would have called it foolishness for a man with not a penny, his means stolen, to name the day.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THREE THOUSAND DOLLARS WAS STOLEN FROM THE SAFE. THEY ASKED FOR THAT SUM BACK.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Remarkable Promise."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 21, "Boldness at The Throne of Grace," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"O GOD! we would not speak to Thee as from a distance, nor stand like trembling Israel under the law at a distance from the burning mount, for we have not come unto Mount Sinai, but unto Mount Sion and that is a place for holy joy and thankfulness, and not for terror and bondage. Blessed be Thy name, O Lord! We have learnt to call Thee “Our Father, which art in heaven”; so there is reverence, for Thou art in heaven, but there is sweet familiarity, for Thou art our Father."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: O GOD! WE WOULD NOT SPEAK TO THEE AS FROM A DISTANCE
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A man and his wife were out of work and in great trouble. Mr. H., a missionary, had already searched among families he knew. After two fruitless weeks he said, "Well, John, let us go into the Fulton Street meeting and leave it with the Lord." They did. The request was read and remembered.

The next day Mr. H. received a note from one of the families he had already asked, without success, requesting him to send the man and wife he had spoken of. He did, and both were engaged. He counted it a marked answer, because it was hard to find a family that wanted a man and a woman servant, and that particular family had seemed the least likely.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: TWO WEEKS OF ASKING DOOR TO DOOR. THEN THEY TOOK IT INTO THE NOON MEETING.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Employment Found."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 228:

"As thou hast thought, so let it come to pass, and as thou hast purposed, let it stand."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Which of our plans are we asking him to protect against his purpose?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 228. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text: Dr. Newman Hall of Surrey Chapel, London, told of his brother, a Sunday-school superintendent, who on a Saturday evening felt a strong impulse to call on a member of his Bible class he had never visited, and to ask if he was in any need. He found the young man very ill. The mother and sister seemed comfortable, but when he asked if he could help, they burst into tears. The young man had been asking for food they could not supply, and on Monday some of their goods were to be taken for unpaid rates. When he knocked, they were on their knees praying for help. A few friends met the difficulty at once. Hall said the timely help was felt to be the direct answer to that prayer.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HE KNOCKED BECAUSE HE FELT HE SHOULD. THEY WERE ON THEIR KNEES WHEN HE KNOCKED.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Answers To Prayer."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Rev. Frederick G. Clark wrote of a woman in his first charge whose love for the Bible was remarkable. Twenty-seven years before she told him, she had read a chapter or half a chapter with little interest. She was already serious about religious things, but Baxter, Payson, and Robert Phillips kindled her more than Scripture. She read the Bible from duty, then turned to those books.

She grew grieved about that and prayed to love the Bible. Clark says some time passed before she felt the request was granted. Then a strange light came over the page. A fascination held her. She found a depth and a charm that were new. Sometimes, after she had closed the book and started toward bed, she went back for a few more verses.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE READ THE BIBLE FROM DUTY, THEN TURNED TO OTHER BOOKS FOR THE FIRE.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("How She Learned To Love The Bible."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 22, "The Presence of God," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR Father, which art in heaven, our hearts are full of gratitude to Thee for Thy Word. We bless Thee that we have it in our houses, that Thou hast given to many of us to understand it and to enjoy it. Although as yet we know not what we shall know, yet have we learned from it what we never can forget, that which has changed our lives has removed our burdens, has comforted our hearts, has set our faces like flints against sin, and made us eager after perfect holiness."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR FATHER, WHICH ART IN HEAVEN, OUR HEARTS ARE FULL OF GRATITUDE
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A missionary and his wife in Northern Mexico supported themselves for nearly four years by teaching and by whatever way the Lord opened. Their schools were Protestant, and he preached regularly. Romanist opposition was strong, and the people were extremely poor, so the income was small. Often only the children of the poorest were permitted to come. They never turned those away, though they could pay no tuition.

Early in 1869 they asked the Lord to make his will known and to provide what they needed. In about three weeks a check arrived. Later, just after family worship one evening, a rap came. A company of people came in, each bearing something, exactly the things most needed, to the amount of over fifty dollars' worth. About a sixth of it, they learned, was given by Romanists who had opposed them the whole time.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THE SCHOOLS WERE PROTESTANT. OFTEN ONLY THE POOREST CHILDREN WERE ALLOWED TO COME.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("A Missionary's Experience In Mexico."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 59:

"Thou puttest no trust in thy saints, and the heavens are not clean in thy sight: How much more abominable and filthy is man, who drinketh iniquity like waters!"
Alt text(s): Question card reading: If the heavens are not clean in his sight, what are we trusting in ourselves?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 59. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
In the fall of 1858, H., a student at Princeton Theological Seminary, needed boots. His toes were sticking out of the old ones, and the money he had would barely pay his fare home, where he had promised a friend to be present on the coming communion Sabbath.

He asked God for a pair of boots before that Sabbath. Saturday morning came and there was still no answer. He started home anyway, persuaded the request would be granted in time. A merchant he knew asked after him and then asked him to go to a certain boot and shoe store, pick as good a pair as he could find, and charge them to the merchant. H. told the writer, back at the seminary, that it was a direct answer. The account says he went through college and seminary on prayer, laid his plans before God, and was not disappointed.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: HIS TOES WERE OUT OF HIS BOOTS. HE ASKED FOR A PAIR BEFORE THE COMMUNION SABBATH.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("Prayer For A Pair Of Boots."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
A disciple, poor in goods and rich in faith, was perplexed by Matthew 5:42, "Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away." After a long time wondering whether it was literal, she said, "It is easy enough to find out; test it and see."

It was Saturday. All but two dollars had gone for the Sabbath, and those two dollars were needed for Monday. She put them in her pocket and went out. A friend whose husband had been out of work met her, told their distress, and asked if she could lend them two dollars to last over the Sabbath.

She was surprised, and she lent them. The book says she was never more astonished, and that she shouted for joy. She had tested the promise. She said she never doubted since, and though often in straits she was always delivered.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: SHE HAD TWO DOLLARS FOR MONDAY. ON SATURDAY A FRIEND ASKED TO BORROW THEM.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("How the Lord Blesses Those "Who Give Liberally to His Cause."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 23, "The Look of Faith," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"OUR Father, we have listened to Thy gracious words. Truly Thy paths drop fatness. Wherever Thou art, mercy abounds. Before Thy feet, rivers of grace spring up. When Thou comest to man, it is with the fulness of pardoning love. Thou hast bidden us come to Thee and seek Thee while Thou mayest be found. We would come now. May Thy Holy Spirit help us! May Jesus lead the way and be our Mediator now! Blessed be Thy name. There are many who sought Thy face many years ago."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: OUR FATHER, WE HAVE LISTENED TO THY GRACIOUS WORDS
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 137:

"That being by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he poured it forth as rivers of living water."
Alt text(s): Question card reading: Are we asking for a trickle from a river he already poured out?
Comment(s): Source: Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710), page 137. Public domain. Quoted word for word.

Text:
A home missionary in Brooklyn had $300 of mortgage interest due in a few days and did not know where to get it. The last night he spent in prayer until he was assured all was well. He asked not to be put to reproach, and not to have his trust dishonored in front of others.

The last moment came with no money. He went to the holder of the mortgage to say he could not meet the demand. As he was about to leave, the gentleman said, "By the way, here is an envelope I was told to give you."

Inside were six fifty-dollar bills, the three hundred dollars he had prayed for. The book says the Lord met him in the jaws of the enemy.

The same bank entry then turns to a different question about bad habits.
Alt text(s): Illustrated scene with the headline: THREE HUNDRED DOLLARS OF INTEREST WAS DUE. HE WENT TO SAY HE COULD NOT PAY.
Comment(s): Source: The Wonders of Prayer (1885), a public-domain collection of answered-prayer accounts ("The Lord Paid His Interest."). Retold here in modern English.

Text:
From Prayer 24, "“Deliver Us from Evil”," in Prayers of C. H. Spurgeon. His words:

"O GOD, let us not be formalists or hypocrites at this time in prayer. We feel how easy it is to bow the head and cover the face and yet the thoughts may be all astray, and the mind may be wandering hither and thither, so that there shall be no real prayer at all. Come, Holy Spirit, help us to feel that we are in the immediate presence of God and may this thought lead us to sincere and earnest petitioning. There are some who know not God. God is not in all their thoughts."
Alt text(s): Prayer card titled: O GOD, LET US NOT BE FORMALISTS OR HYPOCRITES AT THIS TIME IN PRAYER
Comment(s): Source: the recorded pulpit prayers of Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834-1892). Public domain. Quoted word for word.
